title: Boost AMD LLM inference with llama-cpp-rdna-boosts
excerpt: A minimal patch set for llama.cpp raises AMD token generation from 35 to 55 t/s and prefill from 700 to 1300 t/s.
body:
A recent burst of AMD-focused inference forks shows why generic engines often leave performance on the table. The author of the AMD-specific llama-cpp fork measured token generation climb from 35 to 55 tokens / second and pre-fill jump from 700 to 1 300 tokens / second after applying the patches. Those numbers illustrate the gap between a one-size-fits-all engine and a version tuned for RDNA hardware.

The reader will learn why broad-compatibility engines fall short on AMD GPUs, what exact changes llama-cpp-rdna-boosts introduces, and how to run the pre-built container with podman on an eGPU. By the end, the steps to try the boost on a personal setup will be clear.

## Why generic inference engines fall short on AMD hardware

Most open-source inference projects, llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, target a wide range of GPUs. Their code paths avoid hardware-specific tricks to keep the build simple and the binary portable. The source notes that this “generalist” approach optimizes for compatibility rather than raw speed on any one platform.

When an AMD card runs a generic engine, it must rely on the ROCm runtime’s default kernels, which are not tuned for the RDNA architecture’s wavefront scheduling or memory layout. The result is a respectable baseline but far from the potential ceiling. In contrast, bespoke forks such as Strata or Basalt chase token-generation speed by altering model behavior rather than the hardware path, often at the cost of transparency.

The proliferation of these forks in November 2026 reflects a desire for higher throughput, yet many of the optimizations “are less about hardware-specific changes” and more about model-level shortcuts. That trade-off can produce impressive numbers on paper while hiding the true hardware utilization. A fork that stays close to the upstream llama.cpp codebase, but injects AMD-focused patches, offers a clearer path to measurable gains.

## What llama-cpp-rdna-boosts changes and how they are applied

The rdna-boosts repository is a set of small patches applied to a pinned llama.cpp commit. Because the changes are minimal, they can be re-applied to newer upstream versions without a full merge conflict. The documentation lists the patches, and each one targets a concrete ROCm or RDNA inefficiency:

* Kernel launch parameters are adjusted to match RDNA wavefront size, reducing idle lanes.  
* Memory copy patterns are reordered to exploit the AMD cache hierarchy, cutting latency during pre-fill.  
* The token-generation loop uses a tighter synchronization primitive that aligns with ROCm’s event model, shaving a few microseconds per token.

Fewer moving parts mean fewer things to maintain, and the patches are transparent enough to be audited. If ROCm libraries are present, the image can be built from source, but the project also supplies pre-built containers that already contain the patched llama.cpp binary.

## Running the pre-built image with podman on an eGPU

For developers who prefer not to compile, the project publishes a ready-to-run image. The pull command is a concrete example:

```bash
podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1
```

Once the image is cached, the inference server starts with a podman run line that exposes the GPU devices and mounts a local model directory:

```bash
podman run --rm -it \
  --network=host \
  --device /dev/kfd \
  --device /dev/dri \
  --group-add video \
  -v "$HOME/models:/models" \
  ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1
```

The author’s launch script adds a few extra flags, but the essential parts are the device mappings (`/dev/kfd` and `/dev/dri`) and the volume mount for the model files. On an AMD R9700 connected via an eGPU, the container delivered the token-generation and pre-fill improvements reported earlier when serving the `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF` model with MTP enabled.

Updating to a newer boost version should be as simple as pulling a newer tag, although the author has not yet tested that workflow.

## The takeaway

Generic inference engines sacrifice AMD-specific performance for broad compatibility. The llama-cpp-rdna-boosts patches target concrete ROCm and RDNA bottlenecks while staying close to upstream llama.cpp. Pulling and running the pre-built podman image on an eGPU provides an immediate speed boost, making it a practical first step for anyone with an AMD GPU.
